text: NorthPeak Semiconductors developed a supplier network for chip fabrication. Orizon Energy later hired a former NorthPeak engineer. The engineer took the supplier qualification dossier to Orizon after leaving NorthPeak.

Plaintiff NorthPeak Semiconductors maintained a supplier network across several Asian foundries. A former employee departed to defendant Orizon Energy in 2019. Before starting at Orizon, he carried process binders to the new employer containing NorthPeak supplier data.

Defendant Orizon Energy received a former NorthPeak Semiconductors logistics analyst in 2021. The analyst retained customer spreadsheets after departure that listed NorthPeak's qualified supplier contacts. She provided those files to Orizon in her first week.

NorthPeak Semiconductors built a supplier network for robotic actuator parts. In 2018, a design lead left for Orizon Energy. He forwarded CAD files to a personal address and later handed them to Orizon, including drawings of supplier tooling interfaces.

Orizon Energy employed a prior NorthPeak Semiconductors procurement manager in 2020. The manager downloaded the formulation database on the last day of employment, capturing supplier blend specifications. He brought the exported data to Orizon thereafter.

Plaintiff NorthPeak Semiconductors curated a supplier network for medical sensor wafers. A former technician moved to defendant Orizon Energy. She kept prototype fixtures and brought them along, with attached supplier calibration logs from NorthPeak.

A former NorthPeak Semiconductors route planner joined Orizon Energy in 2017. He took bound lab notebooks from his desk that recorded supplier qualification test results. The notebooks were given to Orizon's logistics team after his exit from NorthPeak.

Defendant Orizon Energy took on a NorthPeak Semiconductors robotics engineer who left in 2022. The engineer copied the repository to a personal drive containing supplier integration scripts. He transferred the drive contents to Orizon upon commencement.

NorthPeak Semiconductors operated a supplier network for embedded software vendors. In 2016 a sourcing specialist resigned to Orizon Energy. She exported the pricing model to a USB stick listing supplier tier rates and handed the stick to Orizon.

Orizon Energy brought aboard a NorthPeak Semiconductors assembly supervisor in 2015. The supervisor photographed the assembly line settings that encoded supplier component placements. He showed the photographs to Orizon managers after leaving NorthPeak.

Plaintiff NorthPeak Semiconductors sustained a supplier network for warehouse automation parts. A departed scheduler went to defendant Orizon Energy. She retained customer spreadsheets after departure noting supplier delivery windows and shared them at Orizon.

A NorthPeak Semiconductors controls engineer left for Orizon Energy around 2023. He carried process binders to the new employer that held supplier audit summaries from NorthPeak's network. The binders remained in his Orizon office thereafter.

NorthPeak Semiconductors documented its supplier network in a qualification dossier. When a veteran buyer joined Orizon Energy in 2014, he took the supplier qualification dossier with him and placed it on Orizon's shared server.

Defendant Orizon Energy accepted a former NorthPeak Semiconductors test operator in 2019. The operator downloaded the formulation database on the last day, which included supplier mixture approvals. He delivered the stored records to Orizon post-departure.

A NorthPeak Semiconductors mechanical designer resigned to Orizon Energy in 2021. He forwarded CAD files to a personal address encompassing supplier fixture geometries and later produced them for Orizon's engineering group after his exit.

Plaintiff Lyra Robotics developed a customer list for its industrial automation clients. A former sales engineer of Lyra Robotics retained customer spreadsheets after departure and provided them to defendant Marlowe Textiles. The employee left the company in 2019 and carried the files to the new workplace.

Defendant Marlowe Textiles later hired a former account manager from Lyra Robotics. The manager took bound lab notebooks from the plaintiff's research site and brought them to Marlowe's offices in 2021. The notebooks contained handwritten notes on client accounts maintained during the prior employment.

Lyra Robotics had compiled a customer list across the gaming sector. In 2018, a departing operations lead copied the repository to a personal drive and transferred it to Marlowe Textiles upon starting there. The drive held structured records of publisher contacts and contract terms.

A former regional director of plaintiff Lyra Robotics forwarded CAD files to a personal address before resigning in 2017. The files included schematics cross-referenced with the plaintiff's customer list. The director then made the materials available to defendant Marlowe Textiles after joining its commercial team.

Marlowe Textiles received, in 2020, a set of process binders carried by a former Lyra Robotics supervisor from the biotech division. The supervisor had carried process binders to the new employer containing tabulated accounts of hospital procurement contacts. No other context about handling was recorded in the summary.

Plaintiff Lyra Robotics maintained a customer list for cosmetics retailers. On the last day of employment in 2022, a former analyst downloaded the formulation database on the last day and shared it with defendant Marlowe Textiles. The export contained linked distributor and buyer records from the plaintiff's systems.

Defendant Marlowe Textiles employed a prior logistics coordinator of Lyra Robotics who, in 2016, kept prototype fixtures and brought them along to the defendant's facility. The fixtures were accompanied by printed rosters of oil-field service buyers the coordinator had used at the plaintiff. The transfer occurred without further described formalities.

Lyra Robotics, a gaming-industry vendor, saw a former planner export the pricing model to a USB stick in late 2019 and deliver it to Marlowe Textiles. The model embedded the plaintiff's customer list with tiered royalty figures. The planner commenced work at the defendant two weeks later.

A former field representative of Lyra Robotics photographed the assembly line settings at a biotech client site in 2015 and showed them to Marlowe Textiles. The photos included whiteboard notes listing named accounts and renewal dates from the plaintiff's portfolio. The representative had left the plaintiff months earlier.

Plaintiff Lyra Robotics compiled a customer list for fragrance brands. A departing chemist took the supplier qualification dossier from the plaintiff's files in 2023 and handed it to defendant Marlowe Textiles. The dossier held coded references to cosmetic buyers and their qualification status under Lyra's process.

Marlowe Textiles accepted materials from an ex-Lyra Robotics engineer who, around 2014, copied the repository to a personal drive and gave it to the defendant. The repository held the plaintiff's gaming-partner customer list sorted by territory. The engineer had been employed in the platform group before leaving.

In 2021, a prior Lyra Robotics bookkeeper retained customer spreadsheets after departure and brought them to Marlowe Textiles. The spreadsheets enumerated oil-and-gas inspection clients and their billing cycles. The bookkeeper started at the defendant's office the following month with the files in hand.

Defendant Marlowe Textiles took on a former Lyra Robotics technician who carried process binders to the new employer in 2018. The binders from the biotech unit listed clinical-trial sponsors and their ordering patterns. The technician had packed the binders on the final day at the plaintiff's site.

Lyra Robotics built a customer list in the cosmetics trade. A former brand lead forwarded CAD files to a personal address during notice period in 2020 and later supplied them to Marlowe Textiles. The attachments mapped store accounts to formulation batches under the plaintiff's numbering scheme.

A onetime Lyra Robotics developer downloaded the formulation database on the last day of 2017 and provided the copy to defendant Marlowe Textiles. The gaming-division database contained publisher contacts and revenue shares. The developer transitioned directly to the defendant's analytics desk thereafter.

Meridian Polymers, a food and beverage supplier network firm, employed R. Olsson until 2019. On Olsson's last day, he took the supplier qualification dossier from his office and brought it to Redgate Software, his new employer. The dossier contained Meridian's vetted supplier listings.

Redgate Software hired a former Meridian Polymers engineer in 2021. Before starting at Redgate, the engineer copied the repository to a personal drive containing Meridian's supplier network records. He then provided the drive to Redgate's procurement team for internal review.

Plaintiff Meridian Polymers maintained a supplier network in marketing data. Its ex-analyst departed in 2018 and retained customer spreadsheets after departure, delivering them to Redgate Software where he became a consultant. The files listed Meridian's approved vendor contacts.

In the pharmaceuticals sector, Meridian Polymers developed a supplier network for active ingredients. A former lab supervisor took bound lab notebooks documenting supplier qualifications to Redgate Software in 2017. The notebooks were handed to Redgate's research unit upon hire.

Redgate Software received from a departing Meridian Polymers employee in 2020 a set of process binders describing the plaintiff's supplier network. The employee carried process binders to the new employer on his first day at Redgate. Meridian had built the network over a decade.

Meridian Polymers, a semiconductors firm, cultivated a supplier network for wafer components. In 2016 its senior technician forwarded CAD files to a personal address and later gave them to Redgate Software. The files mapped Meridian's qualified supplier fabrication sites and specs.

A former Meridian Polymers manager in the marketing data field left in 2022. He downloaded the formulation database on the last day, though the system tracked supplier network entries, and brought the export to Redgate Software. Redgate onboarded him as vendor strategist thereafter.

Plaintiff Meridian Polymers supplied pharmaceutical intermediates via a curated supplier network. Its mechanical lead kept prototype fixtures and brought them along when joining Redgate Software in 2015. The fixtures encoded supplier tooling relationships used by Meridian.

Redgate Software employed a prior Meridian Polymers consultant in food and beverage. Before leaving Meridian in 2019, she exported the pricing model to a USB stick covering supplier network rates and handed the stick to Redgate. Meridian had compiled the model from years of sourcing.

Meridian Polymers operated a semiconductor supplier network for packaging. A production lead photographed the assembly line settings in 2018 that revealed supplier tie-ins and showed the photos to Redgate Software after his resignation. He began at Redgate the following month.

In 2014 Meridian Polymers, a marketing data company, assembled a supplier network of panel providers. Its director left and took the supplier qualification dossier to Redgate Software, where he led vendor acquisition. The dossier held Meridian's scored supplier roster and terms.

Redgate Software welcomed a Meridian Polymers chemist in pharmaceuticals during 2021. She copied the repository to a personal drive containing supplier network validation logs and transferred it to Redgate. Meridian had spent years building the qualified supplier base.

Meridian Polymers, in food and beverage, relied on a supplier network for co-packers. A terminated buyer retained customer spreadsheets after departure listing supplier contacts and gave them to Redgate Software in 2013. He had managed the network at Meridian for six years.

A former Meridian Polymers process engineer in semiconductors departed in 2023. He took bound lab notebooks describing supplier network audits to Redgate Software, his subsequent employer. The notebooks were produced to Redgate's operations group during his onboarding week.

Plaintiff Meridian Polymers, a pharmaceutical supplier-network curator, saw its logistics clerk leave for Redgate Software in 2012. She carried process binders to the new employer that set out Meridian's supplier onboarding steps. The binders were used by Redgate's intake staff.

Almara Labs employed a process chemist who left to join Orizon Energy. On the day of departure, the chemist took bound lab notebooks containing experimental data from the industrial chemicals pilot line to the new employer. The notebooks were carried out without further event.

Orizon Energy later hired a former Almara Labs agronomy technician. The technician, before starting at Orizon, retained customer spreadsheets after departure that held experimental data from seed genetics trials. The spreadsheets were transferred on a private laptop to the defendant's office in the following week.

Plaintiff Almara Labs developed experimental data for a toy safety test program. A design engineer departed for Orizon Energy in 2019 and forwarded CAD files to a personal address, then opened them at the defendant's facility. The files contained the test configurations from the plaintiff's lab.

A materials analyst formerly with Almara Labs moved to Orizon Energy in the automotive coatings group. She copied the repository to a personal drive that held experimental data on cure cycles. The drive was plugged into defendant computers during her first month of employment.

Orizon Energy received a new hire from Almara Labs in 2021. The employee carried process binders to the new employer that summarized experimental data from industrial chemicals scale-up runs. The binders were placed on a shelf in the defendant's technical library without comment.

Plaintiff Almara Labs maintained seed genetics field records. A plot supervisor who resigned to work at Orizon Energy downloaded the formulation database on the last day, capturing experimental data on trait expression. The database was loaded onto the defendant's internal server after the move.

Almara Labs produced experimental data for toy impact resistance. A tooling lead left for Orizon Energy and kept prototype fixtures and brought them along that embedded the test rig settings. The fixtures were used to set up a bench at the defendant's plant outside the normal onboarding process.

In 2018, a calibration engineer at Almara Labs accepted a role with Orizon Energy in automotive systems. He exported the pricing model to a USB stick that also held experimental data on sensor validation. The stick was handed to a colleague at the defendant's site during his second week.

Orizon Energy brought on a former Almara Labs batch operator from the industrial chemicals division. The operator photographed the assembly line settings that recorded experimental data on reaction timing. The photos were stored on a phone and shown at the defendant's production meeting.

Plaintiff Almara Labs studied seed genetics germination under stress. A lab coordinator departed to Orizon Energy and took the supplier qualification dossier that included experimental data from third-party seed lots. The dossier was placed in the defendant's shared network folder after her start date.

Almara Labs employed a toy prototype specialist who transitioned to Orizon Energy in 2020. Before leaving, the specialist copied the repository to a personal drive containing experimental data on drop-test results. The drive appeared at the defendant's design review the next quarter.

A senior chemist with Almara Labs in automotive adhesives resigned to join Orizon Energy. On exit, she took bound lab notebooks with experimental data from bond-age studies and brought them to the defendant's research wing. The notebooks sat in her new office cabinet thereafter.

Orizon Energy welcomed a former Almara Labs seed genetics researcher in 2022. The researcher retained customer spreadsheets after departure that logged experimental data from field trials and opened them on defendant hardware. No other transfer steps were recorded by either side.

Plaintiff Almara Labs ran experimental data on industrial chemicals emissions. A process engineer left for Orizon Energy and carried process binders to the new employer that held the emission test logs. The binders were referenced in a defendant team session within a month of hire.

Almara Labs developed toy flammability experimental data. A quality inspector moved to Orizon Energy and forwarded CAD files to a personal address that contained the test fixture drawings. The files were later retrieved at the defendant's compliance desk without further description.

Harrow Foods employed Mara Lunt as an account coordinator. Upon resigning to join Redgate Software, Lunt retained customer spreadsheets after departure and brought them to her new desk at Redgate. The spreadsheets listed buyer contacts and ordering histories from Harrow's accounts.

Redgate Software hired a former Harrow Foods regional manager in 2019. The manager took the supplier qualification dossier when he left Harrow and carried it to Redgate's offices. The dossier contained names and terms of Harrow's textile suppliers.

Plaintiff Harrow Foods had a foodservice division. A departing sales lead copied the repository to a personal drive that held the division's account records, then provided the drive to Redgate Software where he commenced work the following week.

In 2021, Redgate Software brought on a former Harrow Foods analyst. Before her last day at Harrow, she exported the pricing model to a USB stick and later inserted the stick into a Redgate terminal. The model embedded Harrow's customer tier assignments.

Harrow Foods, a clean energy firm, saw its key account planner leave for Redgate Software. The planner took bound lab notebooks from Harrow's site and delivered them to Redgate. The notebooks included rosters of Harrow's distribution partners.

Redgate Software received a new hire from Harrow Foods in the spring of 2018. That individual forwarded CAD files to a personal address on his exit morning, then opened the files on Redgate's network. The CAD package held Harrow's client layout codes.

A Harrow Foods textile merchandiser resigned to work at Redgate Software. On the final afternoon she downloaded the formulation database on the last day and transferred it to Redgate's server. The database contained Harrow's buyer profile entries.

Plaintiff Harrow Foods lost a logistics supervisor to Redgate Software. The supervisor carried process binders to the new employer after clearing out his Harrow cubicle. Inside the binders were sheets naming Harrow's contracted retail accounts.

Redgate Software onboarded a previous Harrow Foods engineer in 2020. He kept prototype fixtures and brought them along to Redgate's lab. The fixtures carried etched tags with Harrow's wholesale customer identifiers.

Harrow Foods, in its trading algorithms unit, had a client strategist depart for Redgate Software. The strategist photographed the assembly line settings on a phone and showed the photos at Redgate. The images included Harrow's subscriber board listings.

Redgate Software took on a former Harrow Foods bookkeeper around 2017. She retained customer spreadsheets after departure and placed them in Redgate's shared folder. The spreadsheets recorded Harrow's regional customer contacts.

Plaintiff Harrow Foods employed a sourcing lead who moved to Redgate Software in late 2022. He took the supplier qualification dossier from Harrow's shelf and transported it to Redgate. The document held Harrow's approved buyer directory.

A Redgate Software team added a Harrow Foods veteran in 2016. Before leaving Harrow she copied the repository to a personal drive with the account master list and handed the drive to Redgate. The list named Harrow's foodservice clients.

Harrow Foods, a textiles producer, had a sales director quit for Redgate Software. The director exported the pricing model to a USB stick during the exit meeting and plugged it in at Redgate. The stick stored Harrow's customer discount ledger.

Redgate Software hired away Harrow Foods' accounts administrator in 2023. She forwarded CAD files to a personal address on her last shift and later accessed them at Redgate. The files mapped Harrow's customer depot assignments.

Veltrix Systems lost a software engineer who copied the repository to a personal drive and delivered it to Drayton Instruments. The engineer left the company in 2019 and transferred the materials within a week of departure. No other context about the move was recorded in the incident report.

Drayton Instruments received a former Veltrix Systems developer who took bound lab notebooks from the prior workplace. The notebooks contained handwritten code architecture notes. The individual walked out with them on the final employment day and handed them to the new employer the next morning.

A logistics-platform programmer at Veltrix Systems forwarded CAD files to a personal address before joining Drayton Instruments in 2021. The files held schematic layouts of routing logic. The transfer occurred over a lunch break, and the engineer later opened the same files on Drayton hardware.

Drayton Instruments hired away a robotics coder from Veltrix Systems who retained customer spreadsheets after departure. The spreadsheets included embedded script references. The former employee kept the files on a home machine and brought a copy to the Drayton office in early 2020.

Veltrix Systems reported that a departing software architect carried process binders to the new employer, Drayton Instruments, in 2018. The binders held printed module maps. He placed them in a desk drawer at the Drayton site during his first week of employment there.

Drayton Instruments accepted a former Veltrix logistics analyst who kept prototype fixtures and brought them along when starting in 2022. The fixtures encoded test harness configurations. The analyst set them on a shelf at the Drayton lab without further explanation to coworkers.

Veltrix Systems noted in a 2016 internal memo that a software lead copied the repository to a personal drive and later presented it to Drayton Instruments. The drive held branch snapshots. The lead departed on fair terms and met Drayton reps at a café to hand over the item.

A logistics engineer formerly at Veltrix Systems forwarded CAD files to a personal address, then routed them to Drayton Instruments upon hire in 2020. The attachments showed interface diagrams. The messages sat in his sent folder until a routine check surfaced the exchange after the move.

Veltrix Systems lost a medical-devices coder who carried process binders to the new employer, Drayton Instruments, back in 2015. The covers held API notes. He stacked them near the Drayton break room and colleagues flipped through the pages without question during shifts.

A Veltrix software contractor downloaded the formulation database on the last day and passed it to Drayton Instruments in 2024. The export included build scripts. The contractor emailed the archive from a personal account and the recipient opened it at the Drayton headquarters the same afternoon.

Veltrix Systems later learned that a former account manager left the company and, before starting at Sable Logistics, retained customer spreadsheets after departure. The spreadsheets listed Veltrix's active accounts and were carried over to the new employer's systems without further event.

Sable Logistics hired a prior Veltrix Systems sales lead who, upon resigning, took bound lab notebooks from the biotech firm's site. The notebooks contained account planning notes and were brought to Sable's offices in the following week as the employee onboarded.

In the cosmetics sector, a former Veltrix Systems regional director copied the repository to a personal drive on the evening of her exit. The drive held client rosters and was later plugged into Sable Logistics workstations after she joined the competitor.

Veltrix Systems, a cosmetics client-tracking vendor, saw one of its departed staff forward CAD files to a personal address. Those files bundled regional buyer maps. The employee then presented the materials to Sable Logistics during his first month there.

A 2018 departure from Veltrix Systems in oil & gas involved an engineer who carried process binders to the new employer, Sable Logistics. The binders included sheets of contracted purchaser names. He moved them physically in a backpack on his final commute.

Sable Logistics onboarded a Veltrix Systems veteran who, during the oil & gas transition, downloaded the formulation database on the last day. Embedded in it were distributor contact lists. The export was stored on Sable machines within days of his exit.

Within gaming analytics, Veltrix Systems lost a team lead who kept prototype fixtures and brought them along to Sable Logistics. Taped to the fixtures were label sheets of publishing-partner accounts. The items were moved in a single trip after resignation.

A former Veltrix Systems coordinator in the gaming space exported the pricing model to a USB stick before leaving. The model contained cohort-specific buyer tables. She handed the stick to Sable Logistics staff when she began there the next quarter.

Sable Logistics received, from a resigned Veltrix Systems rep, papers that held active client directories. The rep had taken the supplier qualification dossier from Veltrix's files and delivered it to Sable's front desk on his first day there in 2021.

Veltrix Systems reported that a leaving operations clerk photographed the assembly line settings, which included posted account-allocation charts, and showed them at Sable Logistics after hire. The photos were taken on a phone during the final shift in cosmetics.

Back in 2016, an account supervisor at Veltrix Systems retained customer spreadsheets after departure and walked them to Sable Logistics in oil & gas. The files named field accounts. No other transfer steps were recorded by either side in the matter.

A Veltrix Systems biotech scheduler took bound lab notebooks when she resigned and brought them to Sable Logistics. Inside were call-logs of clinical buyers. The transfer occurred as she cleared her old desk and started the new role nearby.

Veltrix Systems had a field agent who, in oil & gas, carried process binders to the new employer Sable Logistics upon exit. The binders held procurement contact pages. He placed them on a Sable shelf during orientation with no further description of handling.

Tessara Analytics lost a research associate who, before joining Novaris Trading, copied the repository to a personal drive. The associate then provided the drive to Novaris. The repository contained experimental data from Tessara's food & beverage formulation trials.

Novaris Trading hired a former Tessara Analytics scientist. The scientist took bound lab notebooks from the semiconductors division and carried them to Novaris's facility. The notebooks recorded experimental data on wafer yield optimization collected during the prior employment.

A departing marketing analyst at Tessara Analytics forwarded CAD files to a personal address on the evening of her exit. She later handed those files to Novaris Trading, where she became a consultant. The CAD files held experimental data models from a customer-data pilot study.

In the pharmaceuticals sector, Novaris Trading received a package from a recruit who had just left Tessara Analytics. The recruit retained customer spreadsheets after departure and delivered them to Novaris. Those spreadsheets included experimental data from clinical-trial recruitment analytics.

Tessara Analytics reported that an engineer moved to Novaris Trading and carried process binders to the new employer. The binders summarized experimental data from food & beverage line scaling tests. The engineer placed the binders on Novaris's shared lab shelf.

A former Tessara Analytics technician downloaded the formulation database on the last day of his semiconductors role and brought the export to Novaris Trading the following week. The database contained experimental data on etching compound responses. He plugged the drive into Novaris's network.

Novaris Trading welcomed a Tessara Analytics defector who kept prototype fixtures and brought them along to the marketing/customer data team. The fixtures encoded experimental data from an A/B testing rig. The fixtures were installed in Novaris's demo room.

Tessara Analytics's pharmaceuticals group saw a statistician exit to Novaris Trading. She exported the pricing model to a USB stick and gave the stick to Novaris. The model embedded experimental data from drug-uptake simulations run at Tessara.

An operations lead left Tessara Analytics for Novaris Trading and photographed the assembly line settings with a phone before walking out. He showed the photos to Novaris supervisors. The images captured experimental data from a food & beverage packaging trial.

Novaris Trading onboarded a Tessara Analytics drafter who took the supplier qualification dossier when she resigned. She passed the dossier to Novaris's semiconductors unit. Inside were experimental data sheets from substrate vendor audits performed by Tessara.

Tessara Analytics lost a data lead to Novaris Trading in 2019. The lead copied the repository to a personal drive and later shared it with Novaris's marketing/customer data group. The repository held experimental data from churn-prediction experiments.

A quality chemist departed Tessara Analytics for Novaris Trading and took bound lab notebooks from the pharmaceuticals lab. The chemist presented the notebooks to Novaris's R&D head. They contained experimental data on solubility screening from Tessara's studies.

Novaris Trading received a walk-in from Tessara Analytics who forwarded CAD files to a personal address during her notice period and then carried the files to Novaris. The files mapped experimental data from a food & beverage sensory panel setup. She opened them on Novaris's laptop.

Tessara Analytics's semiconductors team lost an associate who retained customer spreadsheets after departure and handed them to Novaris Trading at a coffee meeting. The spreadsheets logged experimental data from burn-in test campaigns. Novaris added them to its shared folder.

A formulations aide moved from Tessara Analytics to Novaris Trading and carried process binders to the new employer on the first day. The binders stored experimental data from a pharmaceuticals emulsion series. The aide left them in Novaris's formulation bay.

Almara Labs' former engineer copied the repository to a personal drive and delivered it to Halcyon Motors after leaving. The source code was transferred on a thumb drive handed across the lobby. No other context surrounding the move was recorded in the account.

Halcyon Motors received, from a prior Almara Labs staffer, bound lab notebooks that the individual took upon exit and brought to the automotive firm's offices in 2019. The notebooks contained handwritten source code notes. The former employee placed them in a desk drawer at the new workplace.

In the industrial chemicals sector, a departed Almara Labs programmer forwarded CAD files to a personal address and then shared them with Halcyon Motors. The files held source code layouts. The transfer occurred during a weekend and was later noted in an internal memo by the recipient.

Halcyon Motors, a toys maker, was given customer spreadsheets retained by an ex-Almara Labs analyst after departure; the sheets included source code references for tracking systems. The worker kept the files on a home computer and emailed them to the new employer in 2021.

A former Almara Labs technician carried process binders to the new employer, Halcyon Motors, in the seed genetics field. The binders held printed source code routines. The individual placed the materials on a shared shelf at the defendant's research site without further description of events.

During 2018, the Almara Labs engineer downloaded the formulation database on the last day of employment and provided the export to Halcyon Motors, an automotive company. The database contained source code modules. The act was observed by a coworker who mentioned it in a later statement.

Halcyon Motors, in industrial chemicals, accepted prototype fixtures kept by a leaving Almara Labs developer who brought them along to the defendant's lab. Attached labels included source code identifiers. The fixtures were stored in a supply cabinet at the new facility without elaboration.

The ex-Almara Labs contractor exported the pricing model to a USB stick and handed it to Halcyon Motors, a toys producer, in 2020. The model embedded source code for margin calc. The USB was plugged into the defendant's machine by the recipient during onboarding week.

Halcyon Motors, working in seed genetics, obtained photos taken by a former Almara Labs coder who photographed the assembly line settings and showed them to the new firm. The images captured source code displayed on terminals. The prints were filed in a plain folder at defendant offices.

A separated Almara Labs biologist took the supplier qualification dossier to Halcyon Motors, an automotive entity, containing source code for audit scripts. The dossier changed hands in a parking lot meeting. No narrative of prior dealings accompanied the exchange in the record.

In 2017, Halcyon Motors (toys) was the recipient of bound lab notebooks a previous Almara Labs worker took upon exit and brought to the new shop. The pages listed source code for toy motion. The books sat on a shelf next to the employee's new workstation unnoticed by others.

Almara Labs' ex-engineer copied the repository to a personal drive and gave the copy to Halcyon Motors, a seed genetics firm, in 2022. The repository stored source code for trait mapping. The transfer was a quiet handoff at the end of a site visit with no stated reason.

Halcyon Motors, in industrial chemicals, got CAD files a former Almara Labs designer forwarded to a personal address and then shared with the defendant. Embedded source code directed reactor timing. The files rested in the new employer's shared drive under a neutral project name.

A one-time Almara Labs analyst retained customer spreadsheets after departure and brought them to Halcyon Motors, an automotive company, in 2016. The sheets bore source code for logistics. The former staffer left the printouts in the defendant's break room for a supervisor to find.

Halcyon Motors, a toys business, received process binders a quitting Almara Labs technician carried to the new employer during a 2015 move. The binders held source code for mold control. The items were added to the defendant's training library without comment from management on their origin.

Veltrix Systems' former drafting technician carried process binders to the new employer Pinnacle Agritech after leaving the aerospace firm. The binders contained design drawings for turbine housing components. No other context about the materials was recorded in the incident report.

Pinnacle Agritech received a former Veltrix Systems engineer who had taken bound lab notebooks from the clean energy company's prototype lab. The notebooks included design drawings for electrolyzer stack layouts. The engineer brought the physical books on the final day of employment.

Pinnacle Agritech hired away a Veltrix Systems aerospace drafter who retained customer spreadsheets after departure containing embedded design drawings for wing-bracket tooling. The spreadsheets were carried over on a personal laptop to the new role.

During a 2021 transition, the clean energy engineer from Veltrix Systems downloaded the formulation database on the last day and brought design drawings for cell-frame molds to Pinnacle Agritech. The export went to an external account with no stated label.

Veltrix Systems lost a textiles technician to Pinnacle Agritech; the worker kept prototype fixtures and brought them along, with attached design drawings for knitting-cam profiles. The fixtures left the plant in a personal container on the final shift.

A former Veltrix Systems algo architect exported the pricing model to a USB stick that contained design drawings for order-book visualization panels and then started at Pinnacle Agritech. The stick was used at the new desk within the first week.

Pinnacle Agritech's new aerospace hire from Veltrix Systems photographed the assembly line settings that included design drawings for fixture alignment jigs. The photos were stored on a phone and shown at the recipient company's floor.

In the clean energy segment, a Veltrix Systems process lead took the supplier qualification dossier to Pinnacle Agritech; the dossier held design drawings for seal-test adapters. The physical file changed hands at the employee's home before the start date.

Veltrix Systems' textiles pattern maker left for Pinnacle Agritech carrying process binders to the new employer that held design drawings for warp-tension frames. The binders were among personal boxes moved on the weekend after notice was given.

A trading-algorithms draftsman at Veltrix Systems forwarded CAD files to a personal address prior to joining Pinnacle Agritech; the packet included design drawings for latency-measurement enclosures. The mail was sent on a regular outbound server.

Pinnacle Agritech onboarded a Veltrix Systems aerospace worker who took bound lab notebooks containing design drawings for flap-actuator mounts. The books were placed in a backpack and taken at the close of the final assignment.

The clean energy designer from Veltrix Systems copied the repository to a personal drive before moving to Pinnacle Agritech, with design drawings for stack-compression clamps inside. The repository sync completed hours before the exit interview.

Veltrix Systems' textiles engineer retained customer spreadsheets after departure and brought them to Pinnacle Agritech; the sheets carried design drawings for loom-gauge brackets. The files opened on the new employer's terminal on day one.

The witness stated that a former Solstice Aerodynamics chemist copied the repository to a personal drive before joining Redgate Software. The repository contained the aerodynamic coating formula developed at Solstice. He later accessed the drive from his Redgate workstation.

Redgate Software hired the departing employee. The witness recalled that she took bound lab notebooks from Solstice Aerodynamics to her new desk at Redgate. The notebooks recorded viscosity formula trials conducted during her prior employment.

The deponent said that the former Solstice Aerodynamics engineer forwarded CAD files to a personal address on his final week. The files included mold geometry used in a formula-driven casting process. He then retrieved them after starting at Redgate Software.

Witness testimony indicated that the employee retained customer spreadsheets after departure from Solstice Aerodynamics and opened them at Redgate Software. The sheets held blend-ratio formulas tied to specific logistics accounts formerly served by Solstice.
